constraints.text: Tourism and China. Tourism is about 40% of GDP (AP, 2024; an RNZ report of the same year says more than half: the conflict is kept, the AP figure is used). Chinese visitors halved in 2024 and were back as the top market in 2025 (19,060 of 57,370 arrivals, January to October), so a market Beijing can switch on and off is also the one the economy needs.

paradoxes.text: Refusing to trade Taipei for tourism leaves the economy exposed to the market Beijing switches off. The 2024 pressure halved the Chinese visitors that tourism needs, and the same market was back as the top source in 2025, so the lever is one Beijing can pull again.

grand_strategy.reading: Palau holds three cards out of proportion to its size: a Taipei recognition that Beijing wants, a US Compact and military access that Washington needs in the western Pacific, and the Forum meeting it hosted in 2026. Its money comes from Washington under the Compact and from tourists, a large share of them Chinese, so the government that refuses Beijing's price depends on Beijing's visitors. The paradox sits at the centre of the card: the cards that keep Palau's standing with Washington and Taipei are the ones that expose its economy to Beijing's pressure.

stances.note: Ally by treaty: the Compact of Free Association, with diplomatic relations and the Compact both dated 1 October 1994 (the Interior list gives the relations date). The 2023 review agreements were enacted in March 2024 with US$889 million for Palau over 20 years through 2043 (Interior release, read). Trend warming: the radar agreed in 2022, the Valiant Shield exercises from Palau and the 2024 renewal all point the same way. Bond affinity: a treaty partnership, with no kinship and no open grievance. Confidence A: a treaty-based relation and an official US release; the Interior relations list was cited by Wikipedia and not opened.

stances.note: Partner by recognition, not alliance: Palau has had diplomatic relations with the Republic of China since 29 December 1999 and no treaty with Taipei, so the grade stays partner, the same reading the atlas gives Tonga's recognition of Beijing. Trend stable: the 2 September 2026 joint statement with Taiwan, the Marshall Islands and Tuvalu, and Taipei's state dinner for President Whipps on 20 May 2025, both framed as deeper ties while Beijing presses. The state dinner item was seen in search results and not opened. Bond affinity: shared resistance to Beijing's pressure, with no kinship. An argument for ally (stable de facto alignment) is open, but it rests on Taipei's own rhetoric, so it is not used. Confidence C: tier 3 press, plus one tier 1 item seen but not opened.

stances.note: Rival, not adversary: Palau does not seek Beijing's disappearance; it refuses a price. In 2020 a Chinese ambassador to a neighbouring country pledged a million visitors if Palau capitulated on Taipei, an offer the president rejected (AP). In 2024 President Whipps said China was weaponising tourism to push Palau from Taipei; Chinese arrivals halved that year. Trend stable: the 2025 rebound (19,060 Chinese arrivals of 57,370, January to October, up 25%) is not read as a thaw, since no source explains it. Bond grievance: the coercion is an open wound in the president's own words. Confidence B: the government statement is tier 1 and was reported by AP (tier 3).
